pages.title: Connected Exercise Path
pages.body:
Begin with evidence and a useful result

Choose the task that matters now: improve a resume for a role you want, OR draft a recurring email you need to send. These are alternatives, not a requirement to do both. Provide your own redacted material or use a clearly labeled sample. Follow the selected exercise through its critique and your decision about revisions.

Carry the work into the next step

For a resume, compare the revised statements with your real experience and the role: unsupported metrics must go. For an email, check the recipient, request and tone before sending it yourself. The shared method is to define the useful result, supply evidence, inspect the proposed approach, and decide what to change after critique.

Check Your Work and Choose What Comes Next explains the basic correction-and-recheck process. Keep the résumé or email’s factual checks here.

Use only the support you need

If a job interview is next, use Interview Coach to rehearse your own answers rather than read a model-written performance. If you will work on the same topic across sessions, use Project Brain; a single email needs no persistent workspace.

Open the exercises

  • Ex01 — Resume Tailorer
  • Ex08 — Email Template Library
  • Ex02 — Interview Coach
  • Ex09 — Project Brain

Follow the selected exercise’s instructions and checks; you choose which corrections to use.

pages.title: Transfer and Optional Reflection
pages.body:
Use the method again

Try a different role or a different email recipient. Keep the method, change the context, and check whether the result still serves that person. Optionally describe what you changed, why it helped, and what you will check next. Keep private source material with you.

Check this changed case

Check that the new version uses the new role or recipient’s facts and does not carry unsupported claims from the earlier draft.

If a correction changes an important fact or behavior, check it again. Reflection is optional: name the change that helped and what you will try next. Keep the useful result; no separate submission or log is required.

pages.title: Reference at the Point of Need
pages.body:
Concepts when you need them

Context is the information the assistant needs for this task: purpose, audience, source material and constraints. An instruction asks it to do something; a source supports a factual claim. Plan critique asks whether the approach fits. Result critique asks whether the output meets the purpose. A fluent answer can still contain unsupported facts. Your decision after critique is part of the work.

A worked distinction

Example: a resume bullet sounds stronger after the assistant adds a percentage you never supplied. Reject the number; ask it to show the real action and result without inventing measurement. Carry the correction into your master resume, not a compulsory prompt log.

Return to the work

Use the concept to make a concrete check or decision in your current artifact. If it does not help, return to the task rather than collecting terminology. Ask your assistant to explain an unfamiliar term using your example, then check the explanation against the source or observed behavior.

pages.title: Connected Exercise Path
pages.body:
Begin with evidence and a useful result

Begin with Venture Problem Hypothesis to name a problem space and the customer community you want to understand. Treat the output as an initial hypothesis. Use Customer Discovery Questions to prepare questions about recent real behavior. Speak with or observe real people before moving to Field Notes; an AI rehearsal cannot supply missing fieldwork.

Carry the work into the next step

Bring actual observation or interview notes into Customer Field Notes. Separate what happened, what you interpret and what remains unknown. Then use Customer Archetype Builder to organize patterns without erasing differences. When evidence is thin or contradictory, keep the uncertainty and plan another observation instead of finishing a polished persona.

For help supplying actual notes as readable text or permitted files, see Give AI Text or a File to Work From.

Use only the support you need

Industry Researcher can add context, Competitive Landscape Map can show alternatives people already use, and Decision Matrix can compare a genuine choice. None substitutes for customer behavior. This path supports early problem learning; it does not claim to replace the separate New Venture Planning course.

pages.title: Reference at the Point of Need
pages.body:
Concepts when you need them

WWMCAD is Chris Myers’s customer-centered approach. Start with the problem space, customer communities, current behavior and a day in the life. Build an evidence-grounded archetype before treating the customer-facing canvas as settled. Operations, costs/revenue and iteration come later. The user, buyer and payer can be different people. A hypothesis is a claim to investigate; an archetype summarizes supported patterns and remaining differences.

A worked distinction

Example: two people describe the same delay, but one solves it with a colleague and the other buys outside help. Preserve both behaviors. Ask about their most recent event and its consequences; do not replace those observations with “Would you buy our app?”

Return to the work

Use the concept to make a concrete check or decision in your current artifact. If it does not help, return to the task rather than collecting terminology. Ask your assistant to explain an unfamiliar term using your example, then check the explanation against the source or observed behavior.

pages.title: Connected Exercise Path
pages.body:
Begin with evidence and a useful result

Choose one audience and an offer you can describe truthfully. Use Landing Page Brief to connect its problem, promise, supporting evidence and next action. If the evidence is only a hypothesis, label it and decide what you need to learn. A completed brief does not prove demand.

If turning the audience, offer and evidence into a request is unfamiliar, see Ask for What You Want.

Carry the work into the next step

Carry the approved audience, offer and evidence into Ad Copy Builder. Keep the landing-page promise and ad promise consistent. Review claims, the call to action and the proposed test before using the material. If the critique exposes a weak offer, revise the brief first and recheck the ad; stronger wording cannot repair unsupported value.

Use only the support you need

LinkedIn Profile Optimizer is optional practice in communicating to a specific audience. It is a separate personal-profile task, not a prerequisite for launching an offer. You decide whether a profile is useful to this work.

pages.title: Reference at the Point of Need
pages.body:
Concepts when you need them

A value proposition states who benefits, what useful change they get and why they should believe the claim. A call to action gives a concrete next step. A comparison is informative when the question and conditions are clear. If audience, price, message and channel all change, you cannot confidently attribute the result to wording alone. Choose the metric for the decision you need to make, and keep limitations visible.

A worked distinction

Example: compare two headlines for the same audience and offer under comparable conditions. Before collecting responses, decide what the result would mean and what it cannot show. An interested click may warrant another test; it does not establish willingness to pay.

Return to the work

Use the concept to make a concrete check or decision in your current artifact. If it does not help, return to the task rather than collecting terminology. Ask your assistant to explain an unfamiliar term using your example, then check the explanation against the source or observed behavior.

pages.title: Connected Exercise Path
pages.body:
Begin with evidence and a useful result

Choose Project Brain for a topic you will study repeatedly, OR Industry Researcher for a bounded question. Do not do both just to complete the path. Provide readable source material and check which sources the assistant can access. If browsing is unavailable, gather current sources yourself; a stored URL alone is insufficient.

For readable-source help, see Give AI Text or a File to Work From. For continuing work only, Set Up a Project for Continuing Work explains the workspace and pasted-context routes.

Carry the work into the next step

Carry the source-grounded understanding into Executive Briefing. State the audience, decision or question, and the evidence they need. Inspect factual claims against the original sources, preserve important disagreement, and make remaining uncertainty usable. Do not treat several summaries repeating the same underlying claim as independent corroboration.

Use only the support you need

Use Presentation from Notes only when a deck helps this audience. Keep source references in the exported artifact and inspect the actual file. A text outline remains a useful fallback when export is unavailable, but it is not a finished slide deck.

pages.title: Reference at the Point of Need
pages.body:
Concepts when you need them

A source is material you can inspect. A citation identifies where a claim comes from; it does not make the claim true. Research distinguishes observation, author claim, inference and unresolved question. An interested source may be useful while still needing qualification. Persistence supports continued work, but you must keep important progress explicit and check what the tool retained.

A worked distinction

Example: a vendor reports a large productivity gain without describing the sample. Attribute it as the vendor’s claim, inspect the method if available, and avoid presenting it as an established result. A briefing can say what evidence would change its recommendation.

Return to the work

Use the concept to make a concrete check or decision in your current artifact. If it does not help, return to the task rather than collecting terminology. Ask your assistant to explain an unfamiliar term using your example, then check the explanation against the source or observed behavior.

pages.title: Connected Exercise Path
pages.body:
Begin with evidence and a useful result

Begin with First Repository and Commit in a new harmless folder you own, or inspect an existing practice repository before adding anything. Keep a known working version. If the code is unfamiliar, use Codebase Explainer before you plan a change; it is a read-only orientation exercise.

Before building for a pull request

If you intend to propose a pull request, use First Pull Request’s setup first: establish the approved base and a separate branch, and preserve unrelated work. Build and test on that branch, then return for the finished diff review. A local-only tool needs no host account.

Carry the work into the next step

Use Build a Personal Tool for one repeated task. Define sample inputs and expected results before implementation. Run the normal, malformed and boundary cases, inspect the output, and correct a demonstrated problem. Then use First Pull Request when you have a host account and appropriate contribution access. Keep the branch focused and check the actual proposed diff.

If a technical step is confusing, Work Through a Problem with AI shows how to ask for one concrete next step. Check Your Work and Choose What Comes Next explains claimed versus actual actions; Git and runtime checks remain in the exercises.

Use only the support you need

A local tool and meaningful commit are useful even if hosting is unavailable. A pull request requires a host and contribution permissions; defer that exercise rather than claim you completed it. This path is a small practical introduction, not the full programming course.

Open the exercises

  • Ex18 — First Repository and Commit
  • Ex20 — Build a Personal Tool
  • Ex19 — First Pull Request

pages.title: Transfer and Optional Reflection
pages.body:
Use the method again

Make one further improvement based on real use. Explain the change, run a check that could catch its likely failure, and prepare a focused diff. Optionally note what failed and what check found it. Keep actual run instructions with the tool instead of relying on a chat’s assurance.

Check this changed case

Run the changed tool and inspect its output. If hosting is unavailable, a checked local change remains useful; a pull request is a separate step.

If a correction changes an important fact or behavior, check it again. Reflection is optional: name the change that helped and what you will try next. Keep the useful result; no separate submission or log is required.

pages.title: Reference at the Point of Need
pages.body:
Concepts when you need them

A repository tracks versions. A diff shows changes. Staging selects what enters a commit; a commit records a local version and reason. A branch holds a line of work. A pull request proposes a branch’s changes for review on a host. Local history alone is not an off-device backup. An exit without an error is weaker than evidence that the output is correct.

A worked distinction

Example: a checklist tool prints “success” but omits a row. A test that only checks whether it ran misses the problem. Compare the expected items with the actual output. Inspect status and the diff before committing; keep secrets and unrelated files out.

Return to the work

Use the concept to make a concrete check or decision in your current artifact. If it does not help, return to the task rather than collecting terminology. Ask your assistant to explain an unfamiliar term using your example, then check the explanation against the source or observed behavior.

Use Workflow Library Builder to extract the working instructions, required context, output checks and known limits. Do not build a speculative prompt collection just to fill a library.

Keep the method with a successful example

Keep the instructions, required context and meaningful output checks together. Preserve the working version; label changes you have not tried. Use the transfer page when you want to test a new case.

For instruction scope and its difference from changing source facts, see Tell the Assistant How to Help You. A library entry is not automatically an account-wide instruction.

Decision Record is useful when the work includes a consequential choice you may revisit. Board of Advisors can challenge a developed decision through several perspectives; it does not supply real experts or create evidence. Negotiation Simulator is separate interactive practice when a negotiation is your task. These options are not a mandatory chain.

pages.title: Reference at the Point of Need
pages.body:
Concepts when you need them

A reusable workflow includes its task, inputs, method, output and checks. A prompt without context can hide assumptions. A baseline is the natural question you would otherwise ask with the same information and capabilities. Compare useful outcomes, not length or elaborate roles. Role-play can expose a perspective but is not independent expert review.

A worked distinction

Example: a template worked for a familiar client because the conversation already held their constraints. In a fresh chat it becomes generic. Add explicit input slots for the constraints and test again; do not assume the assistant remembered them.

Return to the work

pages.title: Reference at the Point of Need
pages.body:
Concepts when you need them

An outcome is a useful change for someone; a feature is one possible means. A user story describes a need and its reason. Acceptance checks describe observable success and relevant failure cases. A roadmap communicates priorities and learning; it need not invent dates. Unknown scores stay unknown. Tradeoffs are choices between benefits, costs and risks under constraints.

A worked distinction

Example: two users want faster reporting, but one needs an audit trail and the other wants a quick estimate. Preserve the difference. Prioritize a bounded outcome with a clear check; do not claim everyone agreed because the generated story sounds reasonable.

Return to the work

Use the concept to make a concrete check or decision in your current artifact. If it does not help, return to the task rather than collecting terminology. Ask your assistant to explain an unfamiliar term using your example, then check the explanation against the source or observed behavior.
